opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that the scope is a lot broader than many of us initially expected.

When we started applying sparse autoencoders to protein language models like ESM, the starting hypothesis was fairly modest. Maybe we'd recover a handful of things biologists already annotate: secondary structure, alpha helices and beta sheets, perhaps some well-known binding motifs. We do see those, and they come out quite cleanly. You get features that light up on specific amino acids, on helical regions, on the transmembrane segments of membrane proteins, on particular catalytic residues.

What surprised us is the long tail. Once you scale up the dictionary, you find thousands of features, and only a fraction map neatly onto existing annotations in databases like Swiss-Prot. Some of the rest are probably noise or redundant splits of the same concept. But a meaningful chunk look like coherent biological concepts that simply haven't been labeled. A feature might fire on a structural motif across protein families with very little sequence similarity, which suggests the model has learned something about shared structural or functional logic rather than just memorizing sequence patterns.

So I think about the scope on a few levels. There are low-level concepts, like residue identity and local physicochemical properties. There are mid-level structural concepts: secondary structure, domains, contact patterns. And there are higher-level functional concepts, like binding sites, post-translational modification sites, and signal peptides. The model seems to represent all three, often in different layers, which loosely mirrors what people have found in language models for text.

The exciting part, and also the hard part, is that the model's concept vocabulary isn't constrained by human vocabulary. That's an opportunity, because some of these features may point to biology we haven't characterized yet, and they give us new hypotheses to test. But it's also a challenge for interpretation. With text models you can read the activating examples and say, "Oh, this is the 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature." With proteins, the activating examples are sequences and structures, and a human often can't eyeball what they share. So we've been using language models to help annotate these features automatically, describing what the activating proteins have in common and then checking whether that description predicts activations on held-out proteins.

The last thing I'd emphasize is that extraction is only the first step. The real test is whether these concepts are causally used by the model. If you steer a feature, say amplifying a feature associated with a periodic helical pattern, does the model's prediction change in a biologically sensible way? We've seen encouraging signs there, which suggests these aren't just correlational artifacts. Long term, that's where this becomes really useful: not just understanding what protein models know, but using those concepts as handles for protein design and for discovering new biology.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts protein features with text features but does not characterize proteins as a more constrained conceptual domain than human language.

r002.rationale: It says scaling up the feature dictionary reveals thousands of features, but does not predict that larger protein models will reveal additional concepts.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that we're still mapping it out. When we started doing interpretability on protein language models like ESM, we weren't sure what we'd find. These models are trained purely to predict masked amino acids across hundreds of millions of sequences. Nobody tells them anything about biology. So the question is, what does the model actually learn in the process?

What we found using sparse autoencoders is that there's a surprisingly rich hierarchy of concepts. At the lowest level you get things you'd expect, like features that fire on particular amino acid motifs or on specific residues in a specific context. But then you go up a level and you find features that correspond to secondary structure, alpha helices, beta sheets, binding sites, transmembrane regions. And then higher still, you get features that track things like protein families, functional annotations, even which organism or kingdom of life the protein comes from. Some of these line up almost perfectly with existing database annotations like Swiss-Prot. Others don't match anything we have a name for, and those are actually the most interesting to me.

So I'd say the scope is quite broad, broader than a lot of people expected. The model has essentially rediscovered a lot of textbook biochemistry on its own. But there are limits. The concepts are constrained by what's useful for predicting sequence. If a property doesn't help the model guess the next amino acid, there's no pressure to represent it. And some things, like detailed three-dimensional dynamics or how a protein behaves in a cellular context, are probably only weakly captured, if at all.

The part I'm most excited about is the unnamed features. If the model has learned a concept that we can't map to anything in the literature, that's either a spurious artifact or it's a real biological pattern that nobody has written down yet. Figuring out which is which is the kind of thing that could turn interpretability into a tool for discovery rather than just a tool for understanding the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes protein concepts as broad but constrained by sequence prediction; it does not compare this domain with human language as a whole.

r002.rationale: The response says the field is still being mapped out, but does not predict that larger protein models will reveal additional concepts.

astra-6.text:
I think the scope is quite broad. A protein language model is trained on sequences of amino acids, but to learn the patterns in those sequences, it can develop representations that relate to structure, function, and evolutionary relationships. So the concepts we might extract range from very local properties—whether a region is hydrophobic, for example—to more distributed properties, such as whether a protein might perform a particular function.

The interesting question is how much of that representation maps onto concepts that biologists already recognize, and how much might capture something that we don’t yet have a good name for. We can use known annotations to help interpret the model, but if we only look for known concepts, we limit the potential for discovery.

And there’s an important distinction between finding a feature that correlates with a biological property and establishing that it actually tells us something mechanistic. Ideally, we would use these extracted concepts to generate hypotheses, make targeted changes to a protein, and then test what happens experimentally. That’s where interpretability could become useful as a tool for biology.

r001.rationale: The response describes protein language models as covering a broad range of concepts, but does not compare that domain with human language or characterize it as more constrained.

r002.rationale: The response discusses possible discovery of unnamed concepts, but does not predict that larger protein models will reveal additional concepts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scope is quite broad, and it’s useful to think about it at several levels. At one level, you have fairly local concepts: particular sequence motifs, or properties of amino acids, like whether a region is hydrophobic. Then you have concepts related to structure, such as whether part of a protein forms an alpha helix or a beta sheet. And at a higher level, you might have concepts associated with function—whether a protein binds to something, or has a particular kind of enzymatic activity.

The interesting question is how much of that organization the model learns just from looking at protein sequences. We can look inside its representations and ask whether there are features that correspond to concepts biologists already recognize. But we also want to leave room for features that don’t map neatly onto our existing vocabulary. Those could potentially suggest new biological hypotheses.

Of course, finding a feature that correlates with a function is different from showing that it actually controls that function. So the next step is to ask whether we can use that understanding to make a change to a protein and then experimentally test whether it behaves the way we predicted.

r001.rationale: The response discusses protein concepts but does not characterize protein language as more constrained than human language.
